caption:
A power line went down outside Washington, DC this week. Data centers in northern Virginia sensed the wobble and switched to their own backup power, and about 3.1 gigawatts of load vanished in about 30 seconds. Voltage spiked across the PJM grid from northern Virginia to Chicago. There was no blackout. There was a lot of flickering.

What did not fit on a slide: at its peak the grid was carrying an extra 3.49 gigawatts of electricity nobody was using, and it took another 11 minutes before it stabilized. The fixes are unglamorous. On.Energy is installing a total of 3 gigawatts of campus-scale batteries at four data center sites, so the grid sees one steady, well-behaved load instead of thousands of machines all deciding at the same instant. ERCOT is going the regulatory route and will require large loads to ride through disruptions instead of bailing out.

The caveat, plainly: nobody lost power, and around 3% of demand is a small share. What makes this worth reading is the direction of travel, not the size of this one event. In 2024 a similar event pulled 1.5 gigawatts off the same grid. This one was twice as large.

Source: techcrunch.com, reporting PJM data, Ting Labs sensor readings and Synapse Energy Economics.

slides.headline: The data centers unplugged. The lights flickered.

hero.label: customers on the grid it hit

slides.unit: gigawatts of demand, gone in 30 seconds
slides.body: A grid has to keep supply and demand matched second by second. **When that much demand walked off, the electricity had nowhere to go.**
slides.evidence: The PJM Interconnection manages grids from New Jersey to Illinois and serves 67 million customers, making it the largest grid operator in the United States. When the power line went down this week, it triggered data centers to switch to backup power, and about 3.1 gigawatts of load vanished in about 30 seconds

slides.title: What it looked like from a *kitchen*
slides.body: No blackout. Just voltage spiking across the grid from **northern Virginia to Chicago**, and **light bulbs flickering** across the region.
slides.evidence: The event caused voltage across the PJM grid to spike from northern Virginia to Chicago, according to data collected by Ting Labs , a startup that runs an IoT sensor network out of people's electrical sockets. The event didn't cause a blackout, but it did cause lights across the region to flicker.

Normally, the grid would only need a few seconds to recover from such an event. But this one took more than 10 minutes because more than 3 gigawatts of data centers stopped drawing power nearly simultaneously.

slides.body: It's the canary in the coal mine.
slides.attribution: Ricardo de Azevedo, CTO at On.Energy
slides.evidence: "It's the canary in the coal mine," Ricardo de Azevedo, CTO at On.Energy , told TechCrunch. These sorts of events involving large loads like data centers are "happening more and more," he added.

slides.title: The share that can walk off is *growing*
slides.body: It has happened before. In **2024**, **60** data centers unplugged together. This week's drop was **twice as large**. Data centers were about **6%** of this grid's load back then. By **2040**: **24%**.
slides.evidence: The mass disconnection this week was twice as large as a similar event in 2024, when 60 data centers simultaneously disconnected, pulling 1.5 gigawatts of load from the grid. Back then, data centers accounted for about 6% of PJM's load, according to Synapse Energy Economics. By 2040, they are expected to make up 24%.
